title: Majestic Victory: The Rook Promotion
summary: Walk down the checking rook’s file, then underpromote to avoid a stalemate defense.

nodes.question: How can a single pawn defeat a rook?
nodes.explanation: The king can cover rook stopping squares while the c-pawn advances, but must avoid a skewer or a pin.

nodes.question: Which piece should the pawn become?
nodes.explanation: A queen would allow ...Rc4+ and a forced stalemate after capture. A rook preserves the winning mating threats.

branches.title: Walk the king down and promote to a rook
commentary: Begin from the complete four-piece source board. White must coordinate king and pawn against repeated checks.
c7 threatens promotion and controls d8.
Rd6+ checks from the side because the rook cannot simply occupy the protected stopping squares.
Kb5 steps down without attacking the rook. White avoids the early ...Rd1 skewer setup.
Rd5+ follows the king with another side check.
Kb4 continues down the board, keeping the pawn ready to promote.
Rd4+ checks again from the same file.
Kb3 keeps approaching the edge where the rook will lose checking room.
Rd3+ is the illustrated final check down the board.
Kc2 finally attacks the rook safely. There is no first-rank room below the king to repeat the earlier skewer.
Rd4 sets a different trap against promotion.
c8=R underpromotes. The rook avoids the queen’s stalemate problem and threatens Ra8 mate.
Ra4 blocks the a-file, preventing Ra8 from checking the king along that file.
Kb3 attacks Ra4 and threatens Rc1 mate by covering a2 and b2. The exact rook-versus-rook position is winning for White; the branch stops before assuming Black’s next sacrifice.
branches.explanation: Kb3 attacks Ra4 and threatens Rc1 mate by covering a2 and b2. The exact rook-versus-rook position is winning for White; the branch stops before assuming Black’s next sacrifice.

branches.title: Choose a queen and fall into stalemate
commentary: The same promotion square produces a very different outcome if White chooses a queen.
c8=Q gives away the forced win because the queen can be drawn onto a stalemating square.
Rc4+ checks Kc2 and attacks the queen on c8, forcing the source’s capture to avoid losing the new queen.
Qxc4 is stalemate. Qc4 controls a2, Kc2 controls b1 and b2, and Black’s lone king on a1 is not in check.
branches.explanation: Qxc4 is stalemate. Qc4 controls a2, Kc2 controls b1 and b2, and Black’s lone king on a1 is not in check.

branches.title: Keep the king too close to the pawn
commentary: Compare an early king retreat that places king and pawn on the same rank.
c7 keeps the winning promotion threat.
Rd6+ asks White to choose the king’s route carefully.
Kb7 gives away the win by lining up behind the pawn on the seventh rank.
Rd7 pins c7 to Kb7. White cannot promote while its king would be exposed to check, and the exact position is drawn.
branches.explanation: Rd7 pins c7 to Kb7. White cannot promote while its king would be exposed to check, and the exact position is drawn.

branches.title: Attack the checking rook too early
commentary: The king cannot attack the rook on the sixth rank as safely as it can later on the second rank.
c7 creates the winning promotion threat.
Rd6+ checks from the side.
Kc5 gives away the win. White’s king is now on the same file as its future promoted queen.
Rd1 sets up ...Rc1+ after promotion, skewering king and queen along the c-file. The selected exact position is drawn; it is not claimed to be lost until White makes a further error.

exercises.prompt: Why does a rook win where a queen draws?
exercises.answer: After ...Rc4+, the queen’s capture on c4 controls a2 and stalemates Ka1. A rook on c8 avoids that extra diagonal coverage and keeps mating threats.

exercises.prompt: Why can Kc2 attack the rook when Kc5 cannot?
exercises.answer: On the second rank the rook cannot get below the king to set up the earlier first-rank skewer. The edge of the board changes the geometry.
